sub: The Eucharistic liturgy of the Syro-Malabar Church: its meaning, its order and our part in it
sec: What the word means

“Qurbana” is the Syriac word for “offering”, from the root q-r-b, “to draw near, to offer”. In the Holy Qurbana the Church offers to the Father the one sacrifice of Christ, and Christ gives himself to us as the Bread of Life.

For the Syro-Malabar Church the Qurbana is not one devotion among others; it is the source and summit of the whole Christian life (Lumen Gentium 11). Every sacrament, every feast and every prayer leads to it and flows from it.
Its roots

The Syro-Malabar Church, heir to the faith preached by St Thomas the Apostle, celebrates in the East Syriac tradition, which it received through its ancient communion with the Church of the East. Its principal Eucharistic prayer is the Anaphora of Mar Addai and Mar Mari, one of the oldest anaphoras in the whole Church, attributed to the apostles of Edessa; the Church has also approved other ancient East Syriac anaphoras for particular days.

The restored Syro-Malabar Qurbana was approved by the Holy See in 1985 and revised later. The Synod of Bishops, with the approval of the Holy See, has laid down a uniform manner of celebration for the whole Church; obedience to the Synod and to the Holy See in liturgical matters is part of our communion.
How it unfolds

1. Preparation and beginning. The priest and ministers prepare at the altar. The celebration opens with “Glory to God in the highest” and the Lord's Prayer, with the response “Holy, holy, holy”. Psalms are prayed, and the hymn “Lakhu Mara” (“To you, O Lord”) praises Christ, the resurrection of our bodies and the saviour of our souls.

2. The Liturgy of the Word. The Trisagion is sung (“Holy God, holy Mighty One, holy Immortal One, have mercy on us”). The Scriptures are proclaimed: from the Law and the Prophets, from the Apostle, and finally the Gospel, received with lights and incense. The homily breaks open the Word. The Karozutha, a litany led by the deacon, gathers the prayers of the people.

3. The Liturgy of the Eucharist. The gifts are brought to the altar while the “Onitha d'Raze” (hymn of the mysteries) is sung; the Creed is professed; the peace is exchanged. In the Anaphora the priest prays the G'hanthas (prayers of inclination) and the Kusapas (prayers of humility); all sing the Sanctus; the priest recalls the Lord's Supper and pronounces his words; he calls down the Holy Spirit on the offering (Epiclesis). Then come the breaking of the bread and the signing of the Body with the Blood.

4. Communion and dismissal. After the Lord's Prayer and the invitation “The holy things are for the holy”, the faithful receive Holy Communion. Thanksgiving follows, and the final blessing (Huttama) sends the people out to live what they have received.
What the Church believes
The Qurbana makes present the one sacrifice of Christ on the Cross; it is not a new sacrifice (CCC 1366–1367).
Under the appearances of bread and wine Christ is truly, really and substantially present, Body and Blood, soul and divinity (CCC 1374–1376).
The Holy Spirit sanctifies the gifts and the people; East Syriac liturgy expresses this strongly in the Epiclesis (CCC 1353).
The Qurbana is celebrated in communion with the Pope, our Major Archbishop and our bishop, who are remembered in the prayers.
How to take part well

Come early, prepare in silence, and follow the movements of the liturgy: standing for the Gospel and the Anaphora, bowing, signing yourself. Answer and sing with the community; the Qurbana is the prayer of the whole people.
Keep the Eucharistic fast prescribed by the Church, receive with reverence, and remain for the thanksgiving. Bring your family; teach your children the responses and their meaning.
The sanctuary and its signs

A Syro-Malabar church is built as a picture of heaven and earth. The sanctuary (Madbaha), raised and veiled, stands for heaven; the nave (Hykala), where the people stand, stands for the world; between them lies the Qestroma, the threshold where heaven and earth meet. The veil is opened at the beginning of the celebration and closed after it: Christ has opened heaven to us.

Above the altar stands the Cross without the figure of the Crucified, often called the Mar Thoma Sliba: the Cross of the risen Lord, flowering at its ends, with the dove of the Holy Spirit. The altar faces east, towards the rising sun, the sign of Christ who will come again from the east (Matthew 24:27). The ancient East Syriac churches also had a Bema in the nave for the Liturgy of the Word.
Forms, vestments and gestures

The Syro-Malabar Qurbana has three forms: the Raza (the most solemn form, for great feasts), the solemn form, and the simple form used on most days. The Synod of Bishops has laid down a uniform mode of celebration for the whole Church: the priest faces the people during the Liturgy of the Word and the concluding rites, and faces the altar, with the people, towards the east during the Eucharistic Liturgy.

The priest wears the kuthina (white tunic), the urara (stole), the zande (cuffs), the zunara (girdle) and the phaina (the large outer vestment, like a cope). Incense, lights, bowing, kissing the altar and the sign of the Cross belong to the language of the Qurbana: they teach with the body what the words say.
Questions people ask
Why do we stand so much? Standing is the posture of the risen, of people ready to go; the East has always prayed standing, especially on Sundays.

Why the long prayers of humility (Kusapas)? Before the holy Mysteries the priest, and the whole people with him, confesses unworthiness and trust in mercy. Without humility no one can come near the altar.

Why is Communion received on the tongue? According to the norms of the Syro-Malabar Church, Holy Communion is normally received on the tongue, as a sign of reverence and of receiving a gift that we do not take for ourselves. Follow the norms of your eparchy.
How often may I receive? Catholics may receive every day; a second time on the same day only within a Qurbana in which they take part.
notes: Anyone conscious of grave sin must make a sacramental confession before receiving Holy Communion (CCC 1385).
Participation in the Holy Qurbana on Sundays and days of obligation is a grave duty (CCC 2180–2181).
Liturgical texts and the manner of celebration are determined by the Church's competent authority; no individual may change them on his own (Sacrosanctum Concilium 22; CCEO c. 657).
Disputes about the liturgy must never be carried on with disrespect to the Holy Eucharist, to the altar or to the Church's pastors.
Catholics receive Communion in Catholic celebrations, except in cases foreseen by Church law (CCC 1398–1401).
The Eucharistic fast before Holy Communion is laid down by the particular law of each Church sui iuris; follow the current norm of the Syro-Malabar Church (CCEO c. 713 §2).

sub: How the Syro-Malabar Church walks through the whole mystery of Christ, season by season
sec: Why the Church keeps a year

Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever (Hebrews 13:8). Yet the Church does not celebrate his mystery all at once. In the course of one year she unfolds it step by step: the promise and birth of the Savior, his manifestation, his fasting and Passion, his Resurrection, the gift of the Spirit, the mission of the apostles, the growth of the Church and the final fulfillment at his coming (CCC 1163–1171).

The liturgical year is therefore not a calendar of reminders. Each season makes present a part of the mystery, so that the faithful may enter it, be touched by it and be changed by it. The East Syriac Fathers loved to say that the Church walks with Christ through the year as Israel walked with God through the desert: feast by feast, fast by fast, towards the promised land.
Sunday, the heart of the year

Before there were seasons there was Sunday. From the day of the Resurrection the disciples gathered on the first day of the week to break bread (Acts 20:7). Sunday is the original feast, the weekly Easter, the foundation of the whole year (CCC 2174–2177).

In the Syro-Malabar tradition each Sunday has its own name within the season (for example, the Third Sunday of Annunciation) and its own set of four readings: two from the Old Testament (the Law and the Prophets), one from the Apostle and one from the Gospel. The Sunday Qurbana gathers the parish as one family around the altar.
How the dates are fixed

Two feasts anchor the year. The Nativity of the Lord is fixed on 25 December. Easter (the Qyamta) moves: it is kept on the Sunday after the first full moon following the spring equinox, according to the rule received from the Council of Nicaea (325).

Most of the year depends on Easter. Counting back: the Great Fast begins on the Monday seven weeks before Easter; the Fast of the Ninevites (Moonnu Nombu) falls a few weeks before the Great Fast; the season of Denha (Epiphany) is longer or shorter according to how early Easter comes. Counting forward: the Ascension on the fortieth day, Pentecost on the fiftieth, and the seasons of the Apostles and of Summer follow.

The year begins on the Sunday of Annunciation that falls between 27 November and 3 December, and ends with the last Sunday of the Dedication of the Church. The Syro-Malabar Church uses two sets of lectionary readings in alternate years; the official calendar published each year by the Major Archiepiscopal Curia tells which set is used.
The seasons of the Lord's coming and manifestation

1. Annunciation-Nativity (Subara). About four weeks of preparation, with the Sundays of the announcements: to Zechariah, to Mary, the birth of John, the revelation to Joseph. The Twenty-Five Days' Fast (1–25 December) belongs here. The Nativity of the Lord is celebrated on 25 December, often with a night Qurbana and, in many parishes, the ancient rite of the fire (Thee Uzhalichu) in which the faithful pass before a fire as a sign of Christ the Light.

2. Epiphany (Denha). Denha means “dawn” or “rising”. It begins on 6 January with the Baptism of the Lord in the Jordan, where the Father, the Son and the Spirit were revealed. In Kerala the night of Denha is kept with lights and the Pindiperunnal, the feast of the plantain stems decked with lamps. The Fridays of this season commemorate in turn John the Baptist, the apostles Peter and Paul, the four evangelists, St Stephen, the Greek Fathers, the Syrian Fathers, the patron of the parish and, on the last Friday, all the faithful departed.
The Great Fast, Holy Week and Easter

3. The Great Fast (Sawma Rabba). Fifty days of prayer, fasting and almsgiving. It begins on the Monday after Pethurta Sunday (the Sunday of “looking back”, of reconciliation before the fast); in many parishes ashes are blessed that day. The Wednesday of the fourth week marks mid-Lent; the fortieth Friday (Nalpathaam Velli) marks the end of the forty days of the Lord's fast.

Holy Week begins with the Saturday of Lazarus (in Kerala homes, Kozhukatta Saturday) and Hosanna Sunday (Oshana), with the procession of palms. On Pesaha Thursday the Church celebrates the Last Supper and the washing of the feet; families break the Pesaha appam at home with milk, remembering the Passover of the Lord. Good Friday is a day of mourning, fasting and the Way of the Cross; there is no Qurbana. Holy Saturday is a day of silence at the tomb.

4. Resurrection (Qyamta). Easter is the feast of feasts. The Sunday after Easter is the New Sunday (Puthunjayar), with the Gospel of St Thomas confessing “My Lord and my God”, a Sunday dear to the St Thomas Christians. The Ascension is kept on the fortieth day.
The seasons of the Church on mission

5. Apostles (Sliha). From Pentecost, when the Spirit came upon the apostles, the Church remembers their mission to the nations. The Dukrana of St Thomas, our Father in faith, is kept on 3 July; it is also kept as the day of the Syro-Malabar Church.

6. Summer (Qaita). The season of fruit: the Church, planted by the apostles, grows and bears fruit in holiness. The Assumption of Mary (15 August) usually falls in this season; many keep the devotional fast of the first fifteen days of August.

7. Elijah-Cross (Eliya-Sliba). Elijah, taken up to heaven, was expected to return before the Day of the Lord; the Cross is the sign of the Son of Man that will appear at his coming (Matthew 24:30). The Exaltation of the Holy Cross (14 September) gives the season its center. The Eight Days' Fast before the Nativity of Mary (1–8 September) is widely kept.
8. Moses (Muse). Moses, who led the people to the edge of the promised land, turns our eyes to the end of the journey: judgment, the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.

9. Dedication of the Church (Qudash Edta). The last four Sundays celebrate the Church as the Bride of Christ, cleansed and adorned for the heavenly wedding. The year ends where history ends: in the Church gathered with her Lord.
Feasts, commemorations and fasts

The great feasts of the Lord are the Nativity, Denha, Easter, the Ascension and Pentecost. Other great days are the Dukrana of St Thomas (3 July), the Assumption of Mary (15 August), the Nativity of Mary (8 September), the Exaltation of the Cross (14 September) and the feasts of the saints of our own Church: St Alphonsa (28 July), St Kuriakose Elias Chavara (3 January), St Euphrasia (29 August) and St Mariam Thresia (8 June), among others.

The traditional fasts (Nombu) are the Twenty-Five Days' Fast before Christmas, the Three Days' Fast of the Ninevites, and the Great Fast. Devotional fasts kept by many are the fast of the first fifteen days of August and the Eight Days' Fast in September. Fasting in our tradition is never only a matter of food: it is joined to prayer, reconciliation and almsgiving.
Living the year at home

The liturgical year is meant to enter the home. Keep the crib and the star in Subara; light lamps at Denha; keep the Nombu as a family, choosing simpler meals and giving the savings to the poor; break the Pesaha appam on Pesaha Thursday; read the Gospel of the Sunday together on Saturday evening.

Name the season at family prayer (“This is the season of the Apostles”), pray for the intentions of the season, and let children know which saints are remembered. In this way the rhythm of the Church becomes the rhythm of the family, and the home becomes a little church.
notes: The obligation to take part in the Holy Qurbana on Sundays and days of obligation is grave; only a serious reason such as illness or the care of infants excuses (CCC 2180–2181).

The exact days of obligation and the rules of fasting and abstinence for the Syro-Malabar Church are laid down by its Synod of Bishops; follow the current particular law and the circulars of your eparchy, especially outside Kerala and abroad.
Fasting must never endanger health: the sick, pregnant and nursing mothers, the elderly and those doing heavy work should consult their pastor (cf. CCC 2043).

Customs such as Kozhukatta Saturday, the Pesaha appam, Pindiperunnal and the rite of the fire are traditions of the St Thomas Christians; they vary between regions and parishes. They are signs of faith, not substitutes for the liturgy.
On the number of seasons: some calendars count Elijah, Cross and Moses as a single season; the official Syro-Malabar calendar is the norm.
The Syro-Malabar Church has no liturgical color code like the Roman Rite; do not judge a season by color.

sub: Why we confess, how to examine our conscience, how to make a good confession, and what the Church asks of us
sec: Christ gave this sacrament

On the evening of Easter the risen Lord breathed on the apostles and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:22–23). Through the bishops and priests, their successors, Christ continues to forgive sins in the Church (CCC 1441–1445).

This sacrament has many names: conversion, penance, confession, forgiveness and reconciliation (CCC 1423–1424). In Kerala we usually say “Kumbasaram”. It is the sacrament of the prodigal son coming home and of the Father who runs to embrace him (Luke 15:20).
Why confess to a priest?

Only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7). But God chose to forgive through his Church: Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive and to retain, which they could not use without hearing the sins (CCC 1461–1462). The priest is not a judge who condemns but a minister of mercy who acts in the person of Christ, the Good Shepherd seeking the lost sheep (CCC 1465).

Sin is never purely private. It wounds the Body of Christ, the Church. So reconciliation with God is also reconciliation with the Church (CCC 1445, 1469). Hearing the words of absolution spoken aloud gives a certainty of forgiveness that our feelings alone cannot give.
Mortal and venial sin

Mortal sin destroys charity in the heart: it is a sin whose object is grave matter, committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1857). Grave matter is specified by the Ten Commandments. Mortal sin, unless repented and forgiven, separates us from God for ever (CCC 1861).

Venial sin weakens charity but does not destroy it (CCC 1862–1863). Confessing everyday faults is strongly recommended: it helps us form our conscience, fight evil tendencies, let ourselves be healed by Christ and grow in the life of the Spirit (CCC 1458).
Examining the conscience

An honest examination is the first step. Some questions, following the Commandments: Do I pray daily? Have I denied my faith or been ashamed of it? Have I used God's name carelessly or sworn falsely? Have I missed the Holy Qurbana or Mass on Sundays and days of obligation without serious reason?

Have I honored my parents and cared for them? Have I been unjust, violent or harsh at home, at work, with servants or employees? Have I harmed life: by anger, hatred, abortion, abuse of alcohol or drugs, reckless driving? Have I sinned against chastity in thought, word or deed, alone or with others, through pornography? Have I been faithful in marriage?

Have I stolen, cheated, taken bribes, failed to pay just wages or debts, wasted money while others are in need? Have I lied, gossiped, ruined another's good name, posted harmful things on social media? Have I been envious, greedy, proud, lazy in my duties? Have I neglected the poor?

Children and young people can ask more simply: Did I pray? Did I obey my parents and teachers? Did I tell lies, fight, use bad words, take what is not mine, cheat in exams, waste time on the phone, hurt anyone?
The three acts of the penitent

1. Contrition: sorrow of soul and hatred for the sin committed, with the resolution not to sin again. Perfect contrition comes from love of God; imperfect contrition (attrition) comes from fear of punishment or the ugliness of sin, and is sufficient for the sacrament (CCC 1451–1453).

2. Confession: telling the priest all mortal sins of which, after careful examination, we are conscious, with their kind and number, as far as we can (CCC 1456). Speak simply and honestly; there is no need for long stories or for naming other people.

3. Satisfaction: doing the penance the priest gives, to repair the harm and restore our habits as disciples of Christ (CCC 1459–1460). Where we have harmed others, we must also make it right: return what was taken, restore a damaged reputation, ask forgiveness.
How to make a good confession
Before: pray to the Holy Spirit for light; examine your conscience; awaken sorrow by looking at the crucifix and remembering God's love.

In the confessional: make the sign of the Cross; say how long it has been since your last confession and, if helpful, your state of life (married, student, priest or religious); confess your sins; listen to the priest's counsel and accept the penance; pray an act of contrition; receive absolution with faith. In the Eastern Churches the prayer of absolution often asks God to forgive the penitent; in the Latin Church the priest says “I absolve you”. Both are true and valid forms of the same sacrament.

A traditional act of contrition: O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended you, and I detest all my sins because of your just punishments, but most of all because they offend you, my God, who are all good and deserving of all my love. I firmly resolve, with the help of your grace, to sin no more and to avoid the near occasion of sin. Amen. (Any approved act of contrition may be used, such as the one taught in your parish catechism.)
After: thank God; do the penance soon; repair any harm done; avoid the occasions of sin; come back regularly, not only when burdened by grave sin.
What the sacrament gives

Reconciliation with God, by which grace is restored; reconciliation with the Church; remission of the eternal punishment due to mortal sin and, at least in part, of temporal punishment; peace and serenity of conscience and spiritual consolation; and an increase of strength for the Christian battle (CCC 1468–1470, 1496).

Many people find that the hardest step is the first one, the walk to the confessional. Beyond it is the joy of the Father: “this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found” (Luke 15:24).
Children, first confession and frequent confession

Children who have reached the age of discretion (around seven) are prepared for their first confession before their first Holy Communion (CCC 1457; c. 914). Parents should go with them and confess themselves; children learn most from what they see.

The saints recommend confessing regularly, for example monthly, and before the great feasts. Many parishes offer confession during the Twenty-Five Days' Fast and the Great Fast or Lent; make use of these times.
notes: Every Catholic who has reached the age of discretion must confess grave sins at least once a year (CCC 2042, 1457).

One who is conscious of mortal sin must not receive Holy Communion without first going to confession, except when there is a grave reason and no opportunity to confess; then an act of perfect contrition must be made, with the intention of confessing as soon as possible (CCC 1457, 1385).

Deliberately hiding a mortal sin in confession makes the confession invalid and adds the sin of sacrilege; the hidden sin and the sacrilege must be confessed. Forgetting a sin is not hiding it: the forgotten sin is forgiven and should be mentioned at the next confession.
The priest is bound by the absolute seal of confession: he may never reveal or use what he hears, under the most severe penalties (CCC 1467; Code of Canon Law c. 983; CCEO c. 733).
Absolution requires real contrition and the purpose of amendment; it cannot be given to one who refuses to give up a grave sin or to repair a grave injustice.

General absolution without individual confession is allowed only in grave necessity (danger of death, or very large numbers with no possibility of individual confession for a long time); grave sins must then be confessed individually as soon as possible (CCC 1483).
Some very grave sins carry penalties whose remission is reserved; if this concerns you, speak to a priest, who will explain the path of reconciliation.

sub: Mamodisa and Thailabhishekam: how we are born into Christ and sealed with the Spirit
sec: Christ commands it

Before his Ascension the risen Lord sent the apostles: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). On the day of Pentecost Peter told the crowd: “Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ so that your sins may be forgiven; and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38).

Baptism is the door of the Christian life and of the other sacraments (CCC 1213). It is called the bath of new birth (Titus 3:5) and enlightenment (Hebrews 6:4): “no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit” (John 3:5).
How it is celebrated in our Church

In the Syro-Malabar Church Baptism (Mamodisa) and Chrismation (Thailabhishekam, the anointing with Holy Myron) are celebrated together, as in all the Eastern Churches. The priest is the ordinary minister of both, using the Myron consecrated by the Major Archbishop or bishop.

The rite unfolds in steps: the reception of the child at the door of the church; prayers of exorcism and the renunciation of Satan; the profession of faith (the Creed); the anointing with the oil of catechumens; the blessing of the baptismal water; the Baptism itself, by immersion or by pouring water three times, with the words “N. is baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit”; the anointing with Holy Myron; the clothing in the white garment and the giving of the lighted candle.

The East Syriac form of the words is passive (“is baptized”): it confesses that it is God who acts, through the hands of the priest. Children usually receive their First Holy Communion later, after preparation in the parish.
What Baptism does

Baptism forgives original sin and all personal sins, with all punishment due to sin (CCC 1263). It makes us a new creation, adopted children of God, members of Christ and temples of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1265). It joins us to the Church, the Body of Christ (CCC 1267).

It marks the soul with an indelible spiritual seal, which no sin can erase; therefore Baptism is never repeated (CCC 1272). The weakness left by original sin remains, and the struggle against sin continues; but the baptized are never alone in that struggle.
The seal of the Spirit

Baptism, Chrismation (Confirmation) and the Holy Eucharist together are the sacraments of Christian initiation (CCC 1212). Chrismation completes baptismal grace: the baptized are anointed with Holy Myron (Chrism), consecrated by the bishop, and receive the Holy Spirit as the apostles did at Pentecost, to be strong witnesses of Christ (CCC 1285, 1303).
Like Baptism, Chrismation marks the soul with an indelible character and is received only once (CCC 1304).
Parents and godparents

Children are baptized in the faith of the Church, and parents promise to raise them in that faith (CCC 1250–1253). Godparents (sponsors) must be practicing Catholics who have received the sacraments of initiation, chosen to help the child live as a Christian. They are not chosen only for family honor.
Choosing a Christian name, often the name of a saint, gives the child a heavenly friend and a model (CCC 2156).
In danger of death

In an emergency anyone, even a non-baptized person, can baptize, if he or she intends to do what the Church does: pour water on the head of the person, saying, “N., I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1256). Inform the parish priest afterwards, so that it can be recorded and the other rites completed.

Those who die for the faith before being baptized (baptism of blood), and catechumens who die with the explicit desire for Baptism, are saved without the sacrament (CCC 1258–1259). For children who die without Baptism, the Church entrusts them to the mercy of God and hopes for their salvation (CCC 1261).
Living our Baptism

Remember the date of your Baptism and celebrate it. Renew your baptismal promises at Easter. Teach children that the font is where they were born as Christians. Visit your baptismal church when you can.
The white garment and the lighted candle given at Baptism are a call: keep the garment clean and the light burning until the Lord comes (cf. Matthew 25:1–13).
notes: Parents should ask for the Baptism of their children within the first weeks after birth and prepare for it; delay without a just reason is not right (CCC 1250; CCEO c. 686; c. 867).
Baptism must be recorded in the parish register; the baptismal certificate is needed for later sacraments, especially marriage.
A godparent must be at least sixteen years old (unless the bishop decides otherwise), confirmed, living a life of faith, and not the father or mother of the child (c. 874; CCEO c. 685).
Baptism validly given in other Christian Churches is not repeated when a person enters full communion with the Catholic Church.
In the Syro-Malabar Church Chrismation is not postponed to a later age as in the Latin Church; a Syro-Malabar child receiving Baptism and Chrismation together has received both sacraments fully.
Children of Syro-Malabar parents belong to the Syro-Malabar Church even when baptized elsewhere; register the Baptism in your own parish and Church (CCEO c. 29).

sub: The sacrament of Christ's healing for the seriously ill and the elderly, as the Syro-Malabar Church celebrates it
sec: Christ the healer

The Gospels are full of the sick who came to Jesus: the blind, the lepers, the paralyzed, the woman who touched the fringe of his cloak. He healed them as a sign that the Kingdom of God had come near, and he took their suffering upon himself: “He took our infirmities and bore our diseases” (Matthew 8:17; Isaiah 53:4).

He sent the Twelve to do the same, and “they cast out many demons, and anointed with oil many who were sick and cured them” (Mark 6:13). The Church has never stopped this ministry. The Letter of James gives its clearest form: “Are any among you sick? They should call for the elders of the church and have them pray over them, anointing them with oil in the name of the Lord. The prayer of faith will save the sick, and the Lord will raise them up; and anyone who has committed sins will be forgiven” (James 5:14–15; CCC 1510).
Who should receive it

The Anointing of the Sick is not only for the dying. It is for any of the faithful who begins to be in danger because of sickness or old age: before a serious operation, in a grave illness such as cancer or heart failure, when the elderly become very weak even without a particular disease (CCC 1514–1515). Children who have reached the use of reason may also receive it when seriously ill.

It may be repeated if the person recovers and falls ill again, or if during the same illness the condition becomes more serious. Do not wait until the person is unconscious. The old habit of calling the priest only at the last moment, and of hiding the visit from the sick person for fear of frightening him, robs the sick of the strength and peace the sacrament is meant to give while they can still pray and receive Holy Communion.
Oil, the sign of the Spirit

In the Bible oil is a sign of healing (the Good Samaritan poured oil and wine on the wounds, Luke 10:34), of strength and gladness (Psalm 104:15), and above all of the Holy Spirit, with whom kings, priests and prophets were anointed. Christ himself is the Anointed One, the Messiah, Mishiha.

The oil of the sick is olive oil (or, if needed, another oil from plants) blessed by the bishop, normally in the days before Easter when the holy oils are blessed for the whole eparchy. In case of real need the priest may bless the oil himself within the rite (CCC 1519; CCEO c. 741). The oil is kept with reverence in the parish church and carried to the sick with prayer.
The order of the rite in our Church

The ancient East Syriac tradition did not keep a separate written rite of anointing for many centuries; the Syro-Malabar Church, after the long period of Latin influence, now celebrates the sacrament with its own approved order in Malayalam, which follows the pattern common to the whole Catholic Church. The details printed in the eparchial ritual books should always be followed; what is given here is the usual outline.

The priest greets the house with peace and sprinkles the sick person and the room with holy water, recalling Baptism. Prayers of repentance follow, and if possible the sick person makes a private confession. A passage of Scripture is read, often James 5 or a Gospel of healing, and the family joins in a litany for the sick, the doctors and those who care for them.

The priest lays his hands on the head of the sick person in silence, as the apostles did, and then anoints the forehead and the hands with the holy oil, praying that the Lord in his mercy will help the sick person with the grace of the Holy Spirit, free him from sin, save him and raise him up. In an emergency a single anointing on the forehead is enough. The rite ends with the Lord's Prayer, Holy Communion when possible, and the blessing.
What the sacrament gives

The special grace of the Holy Spirit gives strength, peace and courage to bear the suffering of illness or old age, and protects against the temptation to despair. It unites the sick person to the Passion of Christ, so that suffering takes on a saving meaning. It forgives sins if the sick person could not make a confession. It restores health if that is good for the salvation of the soul. And it prepares for the passage to eternal life (CCC 1520–1523).

The sick are not useless to the Church. Saint Paul writes: “I am now rejoicing in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am completing what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church” (Colossians 1:24). Saint Alphonsa of Bharananganam, who spent most of her short life in illness, is a Syro-Malabar witness to this hidden fruitfulness of suffering offered with love (CCC 1522).
Viaticum: food for the journey

For those who are about to leave this life, the Church offers, besides the Anointing, Holy Communion as Viaticum, the food for the journey to the Father. Christ said: “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood have eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day” (John 6:54; CCC 1524–1525).

Confession, Anointing and Viaticum together are the last sacraments of the Christian, preparing for the heavenly homeland. When death is near, the priest may also give the apostolic blessing with a plenary indulgence, and the family and priest pray the prayers for the dying, commending the soul to God: “Even though I walk through the darkest valley, I fear no evil; for you are with me” (Psalm 23:4).
How the family can help

Tell the parish priest early when someone is seriously ill, and tell the sick person honestly and gently that the priest is coming to pray and to anoint. Prepare the room: a table with a clean white cloth, a crucifix or the cross, a lighted candle or lamp, holy water, a glass of water and a small piece of cotton.
Keep silence during the rite, switch off the television and phones, and pray the responses together. Children can be present; it teaches them that sickness and death are lived with Christ.
Caring for the sick as caring for Christ

Visit the sick, pray the rosary with them, read the Gospel to them, and help them to receive the sacraments regularly, especially on first Fridays. Parishes of our Church have long organized visits to the sick, palliative care units and Communion ministry by priests and religious; take part in them.

“I was sick and you took care of me” (Matthew 25:36). Every hospital bed and every bedroom of the old is a place where Christ waits for us. As Saint Paul says: “If we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord; so then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's” (Romans 14:8).
notes: Only bishops and priests can validly give the Anointing of the Sick; deacons and lay people cannot, though they may bring Holy Communion and pray with the sick (CCC 1516; CCEO c. 739; c. 1003).
Those who are conscious should go to Confession before the Anointing whenever possible; if they cannot speak, the Anointing itself forgives sins when the person is sorry for them (CCC 1532).
The Anointing is not given to those already dead; if it is doubtful whether the person has died, it may be given conditionally. After death the Church prays for the departed.
Every Catholic in danger of death is bound to receive Holy Communion as Viaticum; the parish priest must see that it is not delayed (c. 921–922; CCEO c. 708).

The history of this sacrament in the East Syriac tradition is complex: for a long time the Church of the East used other healing rites, such as the blessing with oil and the Hnana (dust from the tombs of martyrs mixed with oil and water). The present Syro-Malabar order is a post-sixteenth-century development; consult the current eparchial ritual for exact texts.
Pastors and families should never present the Anointing as a sign that all hope is lost; it is a sacrament of healing and strength, and many receive it and recover.

sub: The sacrament of married love and the crowning of a new family in the Syro-Malabar Church
sec: God's plan from the beginning

“So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). “Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Marriage is not a human invention or a mere social contract; it is written into creation by God himself (CCC 1603).

Sin wounded this communion, bringing domination, jealousy and divorce. Jesus restored marriage to its original dignity: “Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate” (Mark 10:9). He began his signs at a wedding in Cana, where he turned water into wine at the request of his mother (John 2:1–11; CCC 1613).
A great mystery

For Christians, marriage between two baptized persons is a sacrament. Saint Paul writes: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), and after quoting Genesis he adds: “This is a great mystery, and I am applying it to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32; CCC 1612–1617).

The Syriac tradition calls marriage a raza, a holy mystery, and sees in every wedding an image of the marriage of Christ the Bridegroom with the Church his bride. The bridal hymns of Saint Ephrem and the East Syriac liturgy sing of the Church as the bride betrothed to Christ at his Baptism and united to him on the Cross.
The marks of Christian marriage

Unity: one man and one woman, giving themselves to each other for life. Indissolubility: a valid sacramental marriage that has been consummated cannot be dissolved by any human power, only by death (CCC 1640, 2382). Fidelity: an exclusive love, without betrayal in body or heart. Openness to life: children are the supreme gift of marriage, and parents are the first teachers of the faith (CCC 1652–1653).

Free consent is the heart of marriage. No one may be forced to marry by parents, relatives or money; consent given under grave fear, force or deception can make a marriage invalid (CCC 1625–1628). The Church in Kerala reminds families that arranged marriages are good only when the young people themselves freely and fully agree.
Betrothal and preparation

Among the St Thomas Christians the wedding is preceded by the betrothal (manasammatham), traditionally celebrated in the church of the bride's parish in the presence of the priest and both families, with prayer and the mutual promise to marry. The banns are announced in the parishes of both parties so that any impediment may be made known.

The Syro-Malabar eparchies require a marriage preparation course, a pre-marriage interview with the parish priest, and certificates of Baptism and of freedom to marry. The couple should go to Confession before the wedding and receive Holy Communion, so that they begin their married life in grace (CCC 1622).
The rite of Holy Matrimony in our Church

In the Eastern Churches the priest is not only a witness: he blesses the marriage in the name of Christ, and this sacred rite, the priestly blessing, is required for validity (CCEO c. 828; CCC 1623). The East Syriac tradition calls the wedding service the Burakha, the Blessing, and ancient forms included the crowning of the bride and bridegroom, recalling the psalm: “you set a crown of fine gold on his head” (Psalm 21:3).

The present Syro-Malabar order usually takes place within the Holy Qurbana or with the Liturgy of the Word. After the readings and homily the priest questions the bride and bridegroom about their free consent, fidelity and openness to children; they give their consent before God and the Church, joining their right hands.

Then come two signs much loved in Kerala. The priest blesses the minnu (the thali), a small pendant traditionally bearing a cross, and the bridegroom ties it around the bride's neck. Traditionally its thread was drawn from the threads of the manthrakodi, the wedding cloth, which is then blessed and given by the bridegroom to the bride, a sign that he will care for her and that she now belongs to a new family. The priest prays the blessing over the couple, asking for love, peace, children and a holy life.
Meaning of the signs

The minnu is not jewellery for display; it is a sign of a covenant made before God and of the faithful love that ties two lives into one. The cross on it reminds the couple that Christian love is a love that gives itself, like Christ on the Cross. The manthrakodi expresses the bridegroom's promise to provide and protect, and the bride's acceptance of a shared life.

The joining of hands, the exchange of rings where it is customary, the blessing and the common reception of Holy Communion all say the same thing: “Love is patient; love is kind” (1 Corinthians 13:4); “It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7).
Living the sacrament every day

The grace of the sacrament remains every day: it gives the spouses strength to love, to forgive, to bear one another's burdens and to raise their children in the faith. A family that prays together in the evening, goes to the Holy Qurbana together on Sunday and forgives each other before sleep becomes a domestic church (CCC 1656–1658).

Married love also means responsible parenthood, respect for the elderly parents who often live in the same house, and fairness between the two families. Pope Francis gave three words for every home: please, thank you and sorry (Amoris Laetitia 133).
When difficulties come

Every marriage meets trials: sickness, debts, migration and long separation for work abroad, conflicts with in-laws, addiction. Seek help early: from a priest, a trusted counselor, the family apostolate of the eparchy, or an experienced couple in the parish.
Christ who was present at Cana is present in every Christian marriage. When the wine runs out, the advice of his mother still holds: “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5).
notes: Catholics must marry according to the canonical form: in the Eastern Churches, before the local hierarch, the parish priest or a priest with the faculty, who blesses the marriage, and at least two witnesses; otherwise the marriage is invalid unless a dispensation has been given (CCEO c. 828; c. 1108).

Marriage with a baptized non-Catholic (for example an Orthodox, Jacobite or Mar Thoma Christian) requires the permission of the competent authority; marriage with a non-baptized person requires a dispensation. The Catholic party promises to remain faithful and to do all in his or her power to have the children baptized and raised Catholic (CCC 1633–1637; CCEO cc. 813–816).

Civil divorce does not dissolve a valid sacramental marriage. Where there is serious doubt about validity, the eparchial tribunal can examine the case and, if proven, declare the marriage null (CCC 1629). Divorced and civilly remarried Catholics remain members of the Church and should be accompanied with patience (Amoris Laetitia, ch. 8).

Dowry and extravagant display contradict the dignity of the sacrament and burden the poor; dowry is also forbidden by Indian law (Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961), and the Church in Kerala has repeatedly asked the faithful to avoid it.
Local customs at weddings (the bride's entrance, the vaazhvu or blessing by elders, the reception) differ from eparchy to eparchy; the essential elements are consent and the priestly blessing.
Marriage between Syro-Malabar and Latin Catholics is a marriage between two Catholics; the rules on which Church the children belong to are given in CCEO c. 29 and c. 111; ask the parish priest.

sub: Bishops, priests and deacons in the Syro-Malabar Church, and the ordinations of the East Syriac tradition
sec: The priesthood of Christ

Christ is the one High Priest, who offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:26–27). All the baptized share in his priesthood: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God's own people” (1 Peter 2:9; CCC 1546). They offer their lives, their work and their prayer as a spiritual sacrifice.

Christ also chose the Twelve and gave them a special share in his mission: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19); “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, so I send you” (John 20:21). Through the sacrament of Holy Orders this mission continues in the Church until the end of time. Those ordained act in the person of Christ the Head, to teach, to sanctify and to shepherd his people (CCC 1548–1551).
Three degrees
The bishop receives the fullness of the sacrament. He is a successor of the apostles, the visible principle of unity in his eparchy, in communion with the Pope and the other bishops (CCC 1555–1561).

The priest is a co-worker of the bishop: he celebrates the Holy Qurbana, forgives sins, anoints the sick, preaches the Word and cares for the people entrusted to him (CCC 1562–1568). The deacon is ordained for service: he proclaims the Gospel, leads the litanies, assists at the altar, baptizes, brings Communion to the sick, leads funerals and serves the poor (CCC 1569–1571).
The essential sign

From the apostles onward the sign of ordination is the laying on of hands with prayer: “They had these men stand before the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them” (Acts 6:6); “Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off” (Acts 13:3). Paul writes to Timothy: “I remind you to rekindle the gift of God that is within you through the laying on of my hands” (2 Timothy 1:6).

In every rite the essential sign is the laying on of hands by the bishop with the consecratory prayer asking God to pour out the Holy Spirit for the ministry (CCC 1573). Holy Orders marks the soul with an indelible character; it cannot be repeated or taken away (CCC 1581–1583). Only a baptized man can validly receive sacred ordination; the Church holds herself bound by the choice made by the Lord himself (CCC 1577). No one has a right to ordination; it is a call from God, discerned and confirmed by the Church (CCC 1578).
The orders of the East Syriac tradition

The Syriac word for the priestly ministry is kahnutha. The East Syriac tradition keeps, besides the three degrees of the sacrament, the minor orders through which candidates pass on the way to the altar: the reader (Karoya), who reads the Old Testament and the Apostle, and the subdeacon (Hewpadiaqna), who serves at the sanctuary. Then come the deacon (Mshamshana), the priest (Kasheesha) and the bishop (Episcopa).

In Kerala a priest was traditionally called Kathanar, and today commonly Achan, father; the old title Malpan was given to priests who taught Syriac and the liturgy to seminarians in the parish schools of the past. The Syro-Malabar Church restored its own ordination rites in the twentieth century, in the line of the East Syriac Pontifical.
How an ordination is celebrated

Ordinations take place within the Holy Qurbana, usually celebrated by the bishop in the cathedral or in the candidate's home parish, with the clergy and people present. The candidate is presented, and the bishop asks whether he is worthy; the people give their consent. The candidate declares his faith and promises obedience to the bishop.

Then comes the heart of the rite. The candidate kneels, the bishop lays his right hand on his head and prays the consecratory prayer, invoking the Holy Spirit. The new priest is vested in the vestments proper to his order and receives the signs of his ministry; he then concelebrates the Qurbana with the bishop. Details differ for each order; the approved Syro-Malabar Pontifical gives the exact sequence and texts.

At the end, the newly ordained gives his first blessing, and in Kerala families and parishes receive him with great joy. The first Qurbana in the home parish (the puthan kurbana) is a feast of the whole community.
Bishops and the Synod

The Syro-Malabar Church is a Major Archiepiscopal Church sui iuris, governed by its Major Archbishop together with the Synod of Bishops, in full communion with the Pope (CCEO cc. 151–154). Within its proper territory the Synod elects bishops, and the Pope gives his assent; outside that territory, bishops are appointed by the Pope from names proposed by the Synod (CCEO cc. 181–187).
A bishop is ordained by at least three bishops. His symbols include the pastoral staff, the cross and the ring; he wears the head covering of the East Syriac bishop at solemn liturgies.
Celibacy and the priestly life

Before the Synod of Diamper (1599) some St Thomas Christian priests were married, as in other Eastern Churches. Since then the Syro-Malabar Church has kept the discipline of a celibate clergy, which it values as a sign of total dedication to Christ and his people. Questions about married clergy are governed by the particular law of each Church sui iuris (CCEO c. 373).

Priests are formed for many years in minor and major seminaries, in philosophy, theology, the Syriac heritage and pastoral work. They commit themselves to the daily prayer of the Hours, to simplicity of life and to obedience to their bishop or religious superior.
Praying for vocations and for our priests

“The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:37–38). The Syro-Malabar Church has been blessed with many vocations; its priests and religious serve throughout India and in many countries. Every family can pray for vocations and encourage a son who feels the call.

Pray for your priests and bishops every day. Respect them, help them, and correct with charity when needed. “Every high priest chosen from among mortals is put in charge of things pertaining to God on their behalf” (Hebrews 5:1); he needs the prayer and friendship of his community. The risen Lord asked Peter three times for love before saying: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17).
notes: Only a bishop can validly ordain (CCC 1576). The ordination of a bishop without the canonical provision of the Church concerned, in communion with the Pope, is gravely illicit.
Candidates must be freely chosen, mature, of sound faith and morals and physically and psychologically suitable; the Church examines their suitability with care (CCEO cc. 758–762).
The Syriac names of the orders are given here in common Kerala spelling; transliterations differ between books.
The exact form of the minor orders and the sequence of rites follow the current Syro-Malabar Pontifical; this lesson does not reproduce its texts, which should be consulted in the approved edition.

A priest who leaves the ministry remains a priest by the character received; he may be dispensed from the obligations of the clerical state only by the Holy See. In danger of death any priest may absolve validly (CCEO c. 725; c. 976).
Permanent deacons are restored in many Churches; their place in the Syro-Malabar Church is governed by its particular law.

sub: Ramsha, Lelya and Sapra: how the Syro-Malabar Church sanctifies the day and the night
sec: Praying without ceasing

“Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). Jesus “told them a parable about their need to pray always and not to lose heart” (Luke 18:1). From the beginning the Church prayed at fixed hours, as Israel did: “Seven times a day I praise you for your righteous ordinances” (Psalm 119:164); “Evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan, and he will hear my voice” (Psalm 55:17). Daniel knelt three times a day towards Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10); Peter went up to pray at noon, and Peter and John went to the temple at the hour of prayer (Acts 10:9; 3:1).

The Prayer of the Hours sanctifies the whole day and night. It extends to every hour the praise and thanksgiving of the Holy Qurbana; it is the prayer of Christ with his Body, the Church, to the Father (CCC 1174–1178; Sacrosanctum Concilium 83–84).
What it is made of

The heart of the Hours is the Psalms, the prayer book of Israel and of Jesus himself. Around them are hymns, readings, litanies and prayers. In the East Syriac tradition the Psalter is divided into sections (hulale), and the hours are rich in poetic hymns (onyatha, teshbhatha) composed by Saint Ephrem, Narsai and other Fathers of the Syriac Church.

Each hour has its own character: evening thanksgiving and repentance at the close of the day, night watching for the Lord who comes like a thief in the night, morning praise for the light of the risen Christ. The prayer is meant to be sung in two choirs, alternating verses, as the Syriac churches have always done.
The day begins in the evening

Following the Bible, “there was evening and there was morning, the first day” (Genesis 1:5), the East Syriac Church counts the day from evening. A feast therefore begins with the Ramsha of the evening before.

The principal hours are Ramsha (evening prayer), Lelya (night prayer, followed by the Qala d'Shahra, the vigil service) and Sapra (morning prayer). The ancient monastic tradition also had Suba'a (compline) and the daytime hours of the third, sixth and ninth hour. The prayers change according to the season of the liturgical year and the day of the week.
Ramsha, step by step

Ramsha opens with the doxology “Glory to God in the highest” and the Lord's Prayer, which in the East Syriac liturgy is sung with the angelic hymn: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isaiah 6:3). Then the psalms of the evening are sung.

At the evening psalm the lamp is lit and incense is offered, with the verse: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you, and the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 141:2). The hymn of thanksgiving Lakhu Mara, “To you, Lord of all, we give thanks”, is sung, and an evening hymn (Onitha d'Ramsha) proper to the day.

A litany (karozutha) follows, led by the deacon or priest, with the people answering “Lord, have mercy”; then the Trisagion, “Holy God, holy mighty One, holy immortal One, have mercy on us”, concluding prayers and the final blessing (huttama).
Lelya and Sapra

Lelya is the prayer of the night watch. It recalls the wise virgins waiting with lamps, the shepherds of Bethlehem who kept watch, and the women at the tomb before dawn. On Sundays and feasts the vigil is longer, with the Qala d'Shahra.

Sapra greets the morning. It sings the psalms of praise of creation and the hymn of the angels, “Glory to God in the highest heaven, and on earth peace among those whom he favors!” (Luke 2:14). The rising sun in the east is a sign of Christ, the Sun of Justice; for this reason churches of our tradition face east. “From the rising of the sun to its setting the name of the LORD is to be praised” (Psalm 113:3).
Books of our tradition

The ancient East Syriac Hours are found in the Hudra (the cycle of Sundays and feasts through the year), the Kashkol (the weekdays) and the Gazza (the feasts of saints). These were compiled over centuries and used in Syriac by the St Thomas Christians in Kerala until the twentieth century.

The Syro-Malabar Church has published the Prayer of the Hours in Malayalam (the Yamaprarthanakal) for priests, religious and the faithful, with shorter forms for families and parishes. The current approved edition and the eparchial calendar should be used; earlier popular prayer books mixed in many Latin devotions.
The family evening prayer

Long before printed breviaries, the St Thomas Christian home had its own hour of prayer: the evening prayer at the lighting of the lamp (sandhyaprarthana or kudumbaprarthana), when the whole family gathered, the children greeted the elders and all prayed together. In many homes it included psalms, the rosary, the litany and the blessing of the children by their parents.

Begin small: one psalm in the morning and one in the evening; the Lord's Prayer three times a day; the Angelus at noon. Learn the evening prayer of your Church and pray it at home with the family. “For where two or three are gathered in my name, I am there among them” (Matthew 18:20).
Praying with the whole Church

Priests, deacons and religious pray the Hours daily on behalf of the whole Church. When lay people join them, especially for Ramsha on Saturday evening and Sapra on Sunday morning before the Holy Qurbana, the parish becomes a praying community.

Even a small prayer said faithfully at the same hour each day joins the great prayer of the Church, which rises from every time zone without ceasing. In this way the whole day becomes an offering, as the prophet foresaw: from the rising of the sun to its setting a pure offering is made to the Lord's name (Malachi 1:11).
notes: Priests and deacons are bound to pray the Divine Office daily according to the particular law of their own Church sui iuris (CCEO c. 377; for Latin clergy c. 276 §2, 3°).
The Prayer of the Hours is the public prayer of the Church; private devotions are good, but they should lead to the liturgy and never replace it (Sacrosanctum Concilium 13).
The East Syriac names of hours and hymns are given in common Kerala spelling; spellings vary between books.

The exact structure of Ramsha, Lelya and Sapra varies with seasons, Sundays, feasts and weekdays; the outline above is general and the approved books should be consulted for the order of a particular day.
Religious congregations of the Syro-Malabar Church (CMI, CMC, FCC, MST and others) have their own approved forms of the Office in harmony with the tradition.
Where the full Office cannot be prayed, the Synod and bishops encourage at least the family evening prayer; it remains the most widespread form of the Hours among our people.

sub: Holy water, the Mar Thoma Cross, blessings and the popular piety of the St Thomas Christians
sec: What sacramentals are

Sacramentals are sacred signs instituted by the Church which resemble the sacraments: they signify effects, especially spiritual effects, obtained through the prayer of the Church. They dispose us to receive the grace of the sacraments and sanctify the various circumstances of life (CCC 1667–1670; CCEO c. 867).

Among them, blessings come first: blessings of persons, of homes, of work, of meals, of objects used in prayer. Others are holy water, blessed candles, the cross and the crucifix, medals, the rosary, the scapular, and the consecration of churches and altars.
Why the Church blesses

God is the source of every blessing. In the Old Testament the priests blessed the people: “The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you, and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you, and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24–26). Jesus blessed the children: “And he took them up in his arms, laid his hands on them, and blessed them” (Mark 10:16).

Created things are good: “For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected, provided it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by God's word and by prayer” (1 Timothy 4:4–5). A blessing is praise of God for his gifts and a prayer that they may serve his glory and our salvation (CCC 1671).
Not magic, but faith

A sacramental does not work by itself like a charm. Its power comes from the prayer of the Church and from the faith and love with which it is used (CCC 1670). Holy water on the forehead recalls our Baptism; a blessed cross in the home declares that Christ is its Lord; the rosary leads us to meditate on the mysteries of Christ with Mary.

Superstition gives to signs a power they do not have; it is a sin against the first commandment (CCC 2111). Fortune-telling, horoscopes for choosing wedding dates, charms against the evil eye and the like are contrary to faith and must be avoided (CCC 2116–2117).
The Mar Thoma Cross

The St Thomas Christians have always honored the Cross. The ancient crosses carved in stone and found at Mylapore, Kottayam, Kadamattom, Muttuchira, Alangad and elsewhere, with Pahlavi or Syriac inscriptions from about the seventh to tenth centuries, show a cross with flowering ends rising from a lotus, with a dove descending above. The Syro-Malabar Church calls this the Mar Thoma Sliba.

It is an empty cross, the Cross of the risen Lord, the tree of life; it proclaims the Resurrection while not forgetting the Passion. Many families also keep the crucifix, which the Church has long venerated; both are honored. “May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14). The St Thomas Christians make the sign of the cross slowly and fully, and the cross on the gable of homes and at wayside cross chapels (kurishupally) marks the land as Christ's.
Blessings through the year

The liturgical year of our Church is rich in blessings. On Denha (Epiphany, 6 January) water is solemnly blessed in many parishes, and in some regions families keep the night with lighted torches on plantain stems (pindikuthi) and a ritual bath (rakkuli) recalling the Baptism of Christ in the Jordan. On Oshana (Palm Sunday) palms are blessed and carried home.

On Pesaha (Maundy Thursday) families of Kerala bless and share at home the unleavened Pesaha bread (indri appam or kurishappam) marked with a cross from the palms of Oshana, and the sweet Pesaha milk, while the head of the family reads the Passion: a living memory of the Lord's Supper in the household. At feasts of patron saints the flag is hoisted (kodiyettam) and processions with crosses, lamps and umbrellas (muthukuda) go round the church.
Blessings of daily life

Traditional blessings include the blessing of a new house, with the priest sprinkling holy water, placing the cross and lighting the lamp; the blessing of a vehicle, a shop or a workplace; the blessing of the first rice given to a child (choroonu) in the church; and the blessing of children by parents and grandparents before sleep or before a journey.

Ask the priest to bless your home, especially in the season of Denha. Parents can bless their children every night with the sign of the cross on the forehead; it is a priestly gesture of the baptized. Keep holy water at home and use it with a prayer. Before and after meals, at the beginning of a journey, in sickness or fear, a short blessing turns ordinary life into prayer.
Popular piety and vows

The faith of our people is expressed in many devotions: novenas, pilgrimages to Malayattoor, Bharananganam and other shrines, the veneration of relics and images, the Way of the Cross, the rosary in October. The Church values this popular piety and guides it so that it leads to Christ and to the liturgy (CCC 1674–1676).

Vows and offerings (nercha) at shrines, such as the shared meal of the nercha, lighting candles, or walking in pilgrimage, are good when they come from faith and gratitude, never when they become a bargain with God, a show of wealth or a substitute for conversion and for the sacraments.
Keeping the right order

The center of Christian life is the Holy Qurbana and the sacraments; sacramentals prepare for them and flow from them. A home with holy water but without Sunday Mass, or a procession without Confession, has lost the right order.
Teach children the meaning of each sign, so that they do not grow up seeing them only as customs. A blessed object handled with faith and understanding is a small sermon in the home.
notes: Blessed objects should be treated with reverence; when worn out, they are burned or buried, not thrown away with rubbish.

Exorcism in the strict sense may be performed only by a priest with the express permission of the bishop (CCC 1673; c. 1172). Those troubled should first be seen by a priest and, where needed, by a doctor; many troubles have natural causes.
Do not buy or sell blessed objects for their blessing; the price is only for the material.
The dating and reading of the Persian crosses are discussed by scholars; the dates given are approximate.
Customs such as pindikuthi, rakkuli and the Pesaha appam vary by region and family; they are local traditions, not obligations of faith.
Some blessings may be given by deacons and, in the family, by parents; others are reserved to priests or bishops (such as the consecration of an altar or the blessing of holy oils).

sub: How the Syro-Malabar Church accompanies the dead and comforts the living in the hope of the Resurrection
sec: Christian hope before death

“I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live” (John 11:25). For Christians death is not the end but a passage. The body that was the temple of the Holy Spirit will rise again on the last day: “What is sown is perishable, what is raised is imperishable” (1 Corinthians 15:42; CCC 1012–1017).

Therefore the Church accompanies her children to the end with prayer, honors their bodies with reverence, and continues to pray for them after death (CCC 1680–1684). “We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers and sisters, about those who have died, so that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
Praying for the dead

Scripture already praises prayer for the dead, that they might be delivered from their sin (2 Maccabees 12:43–46). Those who die in God's grace but not yet fully purified undergo purification after death, which the Church calls purgatory (CCC 1030–1032).

Our prayers, especially the Holy Qurbana offered for them, almsgiving and works of penance, help the departed. The communion of saints unites the living and the dead in one family of God. The East Syriac liturgy remembers the departed in every Qurbana, and the anaphora prays for all who have fallen asleep in the hope of the resurrection.
At the hour of death

When death comes, the family and the priest pray the prayers for the dying and the commendation of the soul. The eyes are closed, the body washed and dressed with respect, and the hands joined, often holding a cross or a rosary. A lighted lamp and a cross are placed near the body, and family and neighbors keep watch in prayer, reading the Psalms and praying the rosary.
Many families in Kerala keep this vigil through the night. It is a time for quiet prayer and consolation, not for noisy conversation.
The funeral rite in stations

The Syro-Malabar funeral rite unfolds in stations. It begins at the home of the deceased with prayers, psalms and East Syriac hymns of hope; the priest incenses and sprinkles the body with holy water, recalling Baptism.

Then comes the procession to the church, with the cross, lighted candles and the singing of hymns. In the church the funeral service continues with readings, prayers and, as a rule, the Holy Qurbana for the departed. Traditionally a lay person's body is placed with the feet towards the altar, while a priest's is placed facing the people, as he faced them in life; customs vary.

Finally comes the burial at the cemetery, where the grave is blessed, the last prayers are said and earth is cast upon the coffin. The body is laid facing east, awaiting the Lord who will come from the east: “For as the lightning comes from the east and flashes as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matthew 24:27).
The hymns of the Syriac tradition

The funeral hymns of our tradition, many attributed to Saint Ephrem and the Syriac Fathers, are among the most moving prayers of the Church. They speak with the departed, comfort the mourners and proclaim the victory of Christ: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Corinthians 15:55).

The office for the departed, popularly called oppees, is sung at the funeral and on days of remembrance. The funeral of priests and of children has its own forms: for a child who died before the use of reason, the Church sings thanksgiving and trust, not prayers for the forgiveness of sins.
Days of remembrance

After the funeral, families traditionally keep days of remembrance with Holy Qurbana and prayer on days fixed by local custom, such as the seventh day, the thirtieth or forty-first day, and the yearly anniversary (Ormma). On these days relatives gather, visit the grave and share a simple meal.

In the Syro-Malabar calendar the Friday before the Great Fast is the commemoration of all the faithful departed, and November is dedicated to praying for them, with visits to the cemetery and the blessing of graves on 2 November.
Grief and consolation

Jesus wept at the tomb of his friend Lazarus: “Jesus began to weep” (John 11:35). Christian faith does not forbid tears; it gives them hope. Families should be allowed to grieve, and the parish community should surround them with prayer, presence and practical help.

Visit the bereaved after the funeral, not only on the day. Remember the dead by name at family prayer and on anniversaries. Teach children that we will see our loved ones again in Christ, where “he will wipe every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more” (Revelation 21:4).
Simplicity and charity

The dignity of a Christian funeral lies in prayer, not in display. Expensive coffins, decorations and feasts that burden the family are contrary to Christian simplicity. Offer the Holy Qurbana and alms for the departed instead, and help poor families with the costs of burial.
Burying the dead is a work of mercy. Parish funeral societies and volunteers who dig graves, carry the coffin, prepare food for the grieving or care for cemeteries share in a holy work.
notes: The Church earnestly recommends burial of the body; cremation is permitted when it is not chosen for reasons contrary to Christian faith. The ashes must be kept in a sacred place (cemetery or church), not scattered, divided or kept at home (Ad resurgendum cum Christo, 2016; c. 1176 §3).

Funeral rites are not denied to Catholics except in the cases foreseen by law; when in doubt, the bishop decides (CCEO cc. 876–877; c. 1184). Pastors should show special compassion to families in tragic deaths, including suicide, for which the Church prays and hopes in God's mercy (CCC 2283).
The details of the stations, hymns and days of remembrance differ from eparchy to eparchy and from region to region; the approved Syro-Malabar Order of Funeral Services is the norm.
The custom regarding the position of the body in church is a local tradition; it is not a doctrinal rule.
Holy Qurbana may be offered for any departed person; offerings (stipends) for Masses should never be treated as a price.
Organ donation after death, done freely and with consent, is permitted and can be an act of charity (CCC 2296, 2301).
