t: The Story of the Syro-Malabar Church
sub: From the apostle Thomas to a worldwide Major Archiepiscopal Church: two thousand years of the Nasrani faith
sec: The apostle who said “My Lord and my God”

The Syro-Malabar Church traces its faith to the apostle Thomas, the disciple who said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John 11:16), and who, touching the risen Lord's wounds, confessed: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). This confession is the heart of the faith his Indian children received.

According to the strong tradition of Kerala, Thomas landed at Kodungallur (Muziris) around AD 52, preached along the Malabar coast and founded communities at Kodungallur, Palayur, Kottakkavu (Paravur), Kokkamangalam, Niranam, Nilakkal and Kollam, with the half church at Thiruvithamcode: the seven and a half churches. He was martyred near Mylapore around AD 72, where his tomb is venerated. These traditions are not documented in contemporary writings, but early Christian authors already link Thomas with India, and the living memory of the community is ancient and consistent.
The Law of Thomas and the Church of the East

The St Thomas Christians, also called Nasranis, lived their faith as the Marthoma Margam, the Law or Way of Thomas: a Christian life deeply rooted in Indian culture in dress, food, architecture and social customs, and Syriac in liturgy. Tradition speaks of a migration of Syrian Christians under Thomas of Cana in the fourth century, ancestors of the Knanaya community, and of the bishops Mar Sabor and Mar Proth in the ninth.

For many centuries the community received its bishops from the Church of the East, whose Catholicos had his see at Seleucia-Ctesiphon and later Baghdad. From it came the East Syriac liturgy (the Qurbana of the Apostles Addai and Mari), the Syriac language and the Persian crosses. Locally the community was led by the Archdeacon, the head of the Nasranis, while the bishops were mainly concerned with ordination and worship. The Tharisapalli copper plates of Kollam (about AD 849) record privileges given by a local ruler to the Christian community.
The Portuguese and the Synod of Diamper

After the Portuguese arrived in 1498, the St Thomas Christians welcomed them as fellow Christians. In the sixteenth century part of the Church of the East entered into communion with Rome (the Chaldean line), and bishops of that line, such as Mar Joseph and Mar Abraham, came to Kerala. The Portuguese missionaries, however, were suspicious of the Syriac traditions they did not know and sought to bring the community under the Latin Padroado of Goa.

After the death of Mar Abraham (1597), Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes of Goa convoked the Synod of Diamper (Udayamperur) in June 1599. It brought many reforms, some useful, but it also latinized the liturgy, condemned and burned Syriac books it judged erroneous, imposed clerical celibacy and placed the Nasranis under Latin bishops. Historians question its canonical authority and regret its methods; the Church today recognizes the harm done by forced latinization, while honoring the sincere faith of those on all sides.
The Coonan Cross Oath, 1653

Tensions grew under the Latin Jesuit archbishops of Kodungallur (Cranganore). When a bishop from the East, Mar Ahatallah, was prevented from reaching the community, a large gathering of Nasranis at Mattancherry on 3 January 1653 held ropes tied to a leaning cross (Coonan Kurishu) and swore that they would no longer obey the Jesuit archbishop. It was a protest against foreign rule over their Church, not against the Catholic faith as such.

Soon afterwards the Archdeacon Thomas was proclaimed bishop by the laying on of hands of priests, as Mar Thoma I. Rome sent Carmelite missionaries under Propaganda Fide, led by Joseph Sebastiani, and a large part of the community returned to Catholic communion; in 1663 Parambil Chandy (Alexander de Campo) was ordained bishop for them, the first Indian bishop of modern times. The Catholic part came to be called the Pazhayakoor (old allegiance); the others, the Puthenkoor (new allegiance), later received a Syriac Orthodox bishop and the West Syriac liturgy. From them descend today's Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Syrian Churches, and later the Mar Thoma Church, the Malabar Independent Syrian Church and, in 1930, the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church. All are children of the same apostle, and the Catholic Church today seeks fraternal dialogue with them.
Under Latin governance

For more than two centuries the Pazhayakoor Catholics were governed by Latin prelates, either of the Padroado (Kodungallur) or of Propaganda (the Vicariate of Verapoly). They kept their Syriac Qurbana in a latinized form and their Indian customs, but longed for bishops of their own rite.

Their leaders appealed again and again. Mar Joseph Kariattil was made Archbishop of Kodungallur in 1782 but died in Goa in 1786 before he could take up his see; his companion Paremmakkal Thoma Kathanar recorded the journey in the Varthamanappusthakam, the first travelogue in an Indian language. In the nineteenth century the community suffered further divisions when bishops sent by the Chaldean patriarch without Rome's approval, Mar Rokos (1861) and Mar Mellus (1874), gathered followers; Saint Kuriakose Elias Chavara, as Vicar General, worked to keep the faithful in Catholic unity.
Vicariates and hierarchy: 1887, 1896, 1923

In 1887 Pope Leo XIII, by the brief Quod iampridem, separated the Syrian Catholics from the Latin jurisdiction of Verapoly and erected the vicariates apostolic of Trichur and Kottayam, at first under European bishops. In 1896, by Quae rei sacrae, he reorganized them into three vicariates, Trichur, Ernakulam and Changanacherry, under three native bishops: Mar John Menacherry, Mar Aloysius Pazheparambil and Mar Mathew Makil. In 1911 a vicariate of Kottayam was created for the Knanaya faithful.

On 21 December 1923 Pope Pius XI, by Romani Pontifices, established the Syro-Malabar hierarchy, with Ernakulam as the metropolitan see and Mar Augustine Kandathil as the first metropolitan, and Trichur, Changanacherry and Kottayam as suffragans. Changanacherry became a second metropolitan see in 1956. In the following decades eparchies multiplied in Kerala and in mission regions of North and Central India.
A Major Archiepiscopal Church

On 16 December 1992 Pope Saint John Paul II raised the Syro-Malabar Church to the rank of a Major Archiepiscopal Church sui iuris, with the Archeparchy of Ernakulam-Angamaly as its see. Cardinal Antony Padiyara was the first Major Archbishop, followed by Cardinal Varkey Vithayathil, Cardinal George Alencherry and Mar Raphael Thattil (elected in 2024). In 2004 the Synod of Bishops received fuller powers of self-government, including the election of bishops within the proper territory.

Today the Church has some five million faithful, metropolitan sees in Kerala (Ernakulam-Angamaly, Changanacherry, Thrissur, Tellicherry and Kottayam) and eparchies across India, from Kalyan and Faridabad to Shamshabad, which serves the faithful in the rest of India. Abroad there are eparchies in the United States (Chicago), Canada (Mississauga), Great Britain and Australia, with pastoral care in Europe and the Gulf. Its priests and religious serve as missionaries on every continent.
Restoring the liturgy

From the 1930s the Holy See encouraged the Syro-Malabar Church to recover its East Syriac liturgical heritage, freed from unnecessary latinizations (later confirmed by Vatican II, Orientalium Ecclesiarum 6). A restored text of the Qurbana was approved by Pius XII in 1957 and introduced in 1962, and Malayalam soon replaced Syriac as the usual language of celebration. The solemn form, the Raza, was celebrated by Pope John Paul II at Kottayam on 8 February 1986, and the revised Qurbana texts were approved in 1989.

The question of the celebrant's direction, facing the people or facing the altar towards the east, long divided opinion. In 1999 the Synod adopted a uniform mode: the Liturgy of the Word facing the people, the Anaphora facing the altar, and the conclusion facing the people. In August 2021, after a renewed revision of the Qurbana text and with the encouragement of Pope Francis, the Synod decided that this uniform mode should be implemented in all eparchies from the end of November 2021. Most eparchies adopted it; in the Archeparchy of Ernakulam-Angamaly many clergy and faithful, attached to the celebration facing the people, resisted, and the matter has required much dialogue, pastoral patience and papal intervention. Catholics are asked to receive the decisions of the Synod in obedience and charity, and to pray that the Qurbana, the sacrament of unity, may never become a cause of division.
Saints of our Church

Saint Kuriakose Elias Chavara (1805–1871), priest of Kainakary, co-founded at Mannanam in 1831 the first Indian religious congregation for men, now the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate (CMI), and in 1866 the Congregation of the Mother of Carmel (CMC) for women; he opened schools beside churches, printed books and renewed the spiritual life of the people. He was canonized on 23 November 2014 together with Saint Euphrasia Eluvathingal (1877–1952), the Praying Mother of the CMC convent at Ollur.

Saint Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception (1910–1946), a Franciscan Clarist sister of Bharananganam, bore long illness with love and became the first canonized woman saint of India on 12 October 2008. Saint Mariam Thresia Chiramel Mankidiyan (1876–1926), founder of the Congregation of the Holy Family at Kuzhikkattussery, a mystic and servant of poor families, was canonized on 13 October 2019. With them the Church honors the Blessed Augustine Thevarparampil (Kunjachan), apostle of the poor, and the Blessed Rani Maria, martyred in Madhya Pradesh in 1995. “That they may all be one” (John 17:21) remains the prayer of this ancient and living Church.
notes: The tradition of Saint Thomas in India rests on the community's memory, local songs (such as the Ramban Pattu and Margam Kali songs, written down late), and early references in Christian writers; scholars differ on how far each detail can be proved.

The relationship of the medieval St Thomas Christians with Rome and with the Christological debates of the Church of the East is discussed by historians. The Syro-Malabar Church holds that the community kept the apostolic faith; the Catholic Church and the Assyrian Church of the East signed a Common Christological Declaration in 1994.
On Diamper and the Coonan Cross Oath there are different historical interpretations among Catholic, Orthodox and other scholars; this lesson tries to state the facts fairly and without blame.

Rulers of Kerala, including the kings of Cochin and Travancore, generally protected the St Thomas Christians and granted them privileges; the community lived for centuries in harmony with its Hindu and other neighbors.
Figures for faithful and eparchies change; consult the official Syro-Malabar Church directory for the current list and statistics.
The liturgical dispute of recent years is a pastoral and disciplinary question, not a question of faith; it should be spoken of with charity and without contempt for any party.
